articles.title: Information Is Becoming Cheaper. Judgment Is Becoming Priceless.
articles.narrative: This opinion piece argues that while artificial intelligence is rapidly commoditizing information, human judgment is becoming an increasingly invaluable competitive advantage in the commercial real estate industry. The author contends that true expertise now lies in the ability to interpret readily available information, discern critical facts, assess hidden risks, and make superior decisions. Judgment, unlike information, cannot be downloaded or replicated by AI; it must be earned through accumulated pattern recognition, intuition, and contextual understanding derived from continuous learning from successes and failures. The author emphasizes that experience is measured by lessons extracted, not just tenure, and that relentless curiosity and self-analysis will be key for professionals to thrive in the AI era.

Rental rates continued to grow, with the average net asking rent reaching $7.55 per square foot, reflecting sustained occupier commitment despite economic uncertainties.

articles.title: Wall Street landlords find wiggle room in new US housing law
articles.narrative: A new national housing law, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, aims to restrict institutional investors owning 350 or more homes from purchasing single-family houses, but includes significant exceptions. Large landlords can still acquire properties if they undertake substantial renovations, offer tenants a purchase option, engage in institutional-to-institutional transactions, or buy homes specifically developed for rent (built-to-rent). While the law imposes penalties for violations and may encourage stricter state-level bans, it provides enough flexibility for institutional players to remain active in the housing market, particularly through built-to-rent strategies. However, the uncertainty surrounding the law has already impacted investment, with capital providers expected to take a year or two to regain comfort with new acquisitions.

articles.title: How Compass’ new size could spell new problems

A class-action lawsuit has been filed in Florida, alleging that Compass' nationwide transaction fee constitutes a deceptive business practice due to alleged lack of disclosure. While attorneys suggest the legality hinges on proper disclosure, the lawsuit highlights broader concerns about how Compass' increasing market share, which in some cities is projected to exceed 50%, could lead to new legal scrutiny regarding consumer choice, commission rates, and competitive practices. The article also notes other legal challenges, including an antitrust lawsuit filed by Zillow and an investigation by the New York Attorney General's Office into Compass' market share in New York.

articles.title: Events Operator Glasshouse Signs 30-Year Lease for 3 World Trade Center
articles.narrative: Glasshouse, an events and experiential venue operator, has signed a 30-year lease for 66,436 square feet at 3 World Trade Center in New York City. This transaction, structured as a three-party agreement, marks Glasshouse's fourth Manhattan location and is considered one of the most significant experiential leasing deals in the city recently. The new venue is expected to draw over 250,000 visitors annually, enhancing the vibrancy and appeal of the World Trade Center campus and Lower Manhattan.

articles.title: Silver Lake Development Parcel Increases Density Through Re-Entitlement
articles.narrative: A three-parcel development site in Los Angeles' Silver Lake neighborhood, known as Hyperion Residences, was sold for $5.25 million. The buyer, a local affordable housing developer, successfully re-entitled the site during escrow to increase the planned density from 54 units to 105 units, significantly reducing the per-unit cost. This transaction highlights the strong demand for sites that can leverage Executive Directive 1 to achieve higher density in entitlement-constrained areas like Silver Lake.

articles.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of North Shore Industrial Condo
articles.narrative: Marcus & Millichap has facilitated the sale of an industrial condominium in Middleton, MA, for $2,525,000. The property, featuring a mix of warehouse, showroom, and office space, attracted strong interest from both owner-users and investors due to its quality and the low market vacancy in the North Shore area. The transaction highlights the appeal of industrial assets in core markets to investors seeking certainty of execution.

data_points.notable_features: The property includes a 7,025-square-foot warehouse, a 2,975-square-foot first-floor showroom, and a 2,975-square-foot second-floor office space, along with 25 parking spaces.

articles.title: New Housing Law To Send Institutional Investors Flocking To Build-To-Rent
articles.narrative: A new federal housing law, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, is expected to redirect institutional investment towards build-to-rent (BTR) properties. The law prohibits large institutional investors from owning more than 350 single-family homes, but exempts homes built specifically for rental, creating a clear pathway for capital into the BTR sector. This shift is anticipated to significantly impact markets like Atlanta, where institutional investors currently hold a substantial portion of single-family homes, potentially increasing the supply of rental options for households facing high interest rates and inflated housing costs. Developers in the BTR space, who had previously paused projects due to earlier legislative proposals, are now optimistic about ramping up activity.
articles.market_intelligence: Institutional investors control nearly 30% of Atlanta's single-family homes. The pace of BTR development in Metro Atlanta doubled from a year earlier. An April report from the American Economic Liberties Project states that institutional owners control around 72,000 homes in Metro Atlanta, the most of any major metropolitan area in the U.S. A 2023 investigation found 11 companies owned 1,000 or more houses each in Georgia.

articles.title: $30B Investment In Limbo After Attorneys General Sue To Stop Paramount, Warners Bros. Merger
articles.narrative: Twelve attorneys general have filed a lawsuit to block the proposed $111 billion merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, arguing that the union would violate antitrust laws by reducing competition in the entertainment industry. The lawsuit claims the merger would lead to higher prices, lower quality, and less content for consumers, impacting movie theaters and cable distributors. Paramount has countered that the merger is necessary to create a more competitive media company capable of challenging dominant players in the industry and that delaying the transaction would harm entertainment workers.

data_points.project_notes: The proposed merger involves approximately 100 million square feet of real estate globally, including studio space. Warner Bros. owns a 2.6 million SF film and television complex in Burbank, CA, with 31 soundstages and 11 sets on a 110-acre main lot, and another Burbank facility with 16 soundstages. In the UK, Warner Bros. owns a 1.3 million SF complex northwest of London with 350,000 SF of soundstages and a 100-acre back lot. Warner Bros. also has a nearly 3 million SF combined industrial, office, and studio footprint in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Denver Office Market Posts Best Absorption In 4 Years
articles.narrative: Denver's office market is showing signs of stabilization, posting its strongest net absorption in four years during Q2 2026, with tenants occupying approximately 119,700 SF more than they vacated. This positive trend, despite some tenant downsizing, indicates that the period of rapid deterioration has largely passed. Experts anticipate a gradual recovery, driven by declining sublease inventory, limited new supply, and sustained demand for high-quality office spaces, rather than a swift rebound.

In Denver, vacancy rates varied by submarket, with downtown and River North experiencing higher rates (38.6% and 42.3% respectively), while Cherry Creek posted a significantly lower rate of 12.8%.

articles.title: Chicago Fire Stadium Nears $425M TIF Boost
articles.narrative: A city committee in Chicago has approved a $425 million tax increment financing (TIF) boost for the new Chicago Fire stadium at The 78 development. This revised TIF plan will transfer funds from a nearby TIF district to cover infrastructure costs, reducing the financial risk for the developer. The $750 million stadium, privately financed by the team's owner, is expected to open in Q2 2028 and serve as a significant anchor for the long-planned mixed-use development.

data_points.notable_features: 22,000-seat soccer field; anchor tenant for The 78 megadevelopment.
data_points.project_notes: Project broke ground in March 2026. The TIF subsidy is a transfer of $287M over eight years from the Canal/Congress TIF District to the Roosevelt/Clark TIF District.

articles.financing: $425M in tax increment financing (TIF) approved by city committee for infrastructure costs.
articles.market_intelligence: The Canal/Congress TIF District generates over $65M in new TIF revenue annually, while the Roosevelt/Clark District is expected to generate an average of $17M annually over the next 15 years.
